## Why This Is Asked
Tests partitioned StatefulSet upgrades, PDB, and probes in a real CKAD scenario.

## Key Concepts
- StatefulSet partitioned RollingUpdate
- PodDisruptionBudget for minimum availability
- readinessProbe and startupProbe usage
- Resource requests/limits in containers

## Code Example
```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
  namespace: prod
spec:
  serviceName: "cache"
  replicas: 3
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: cache
        image: myrepo/cache:2.0
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "300m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["bash","-lc","redis-cli PING"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        startupProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["bash","-lc","true"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 30
```

```javascript
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: cache-pdb
  namespace: prod
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
```

flowchart TD

- How would you monitor for anomalies during the upgrade?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: CronJobs, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, and scoped RBAC in a real validation workflow.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling and pod template
- InitContainer for tool bootstrap
- YAML validation with yq and a small validator
- ConfigMap-based configuration and result reporting
- Namespace-scoped RBAC with minimal permissions

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-validator
spec:
  schedule: "*/3 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: config-validator-sa
          initContainers:
            - name: init-tools
              image: alpine:3.17
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache yq jq && echo booted"]
          containers:
            - name: validator
              image: alpine:3.17
              command: ["sh", "-c", "validate.sh"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: manifests
                  mountPath: /manifests
          volumes:
            - name: manifests
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: manifests-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle schema evolution and backward compatibility?
- How would you scale the validator for large configs?
- What monitoring would you add for failed validations?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design namespace-scoped automation, RBAC, and progressive release patterns using standard CKAD primitives.

- ConfigMap-driven orchestration

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-roller
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: canary-runner
          containers:
            - name: patcher

## Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace secret management, rotation workflow, and safe rollouts in CKAD terms. Requires RBAC awareness, InitContainers, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Secret rotation via API and patch
- ConfigMap as state store for rotation timestamps
- Rollout restarts triggered by annotation or config change
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
# Skeleton: Deployment (agent) in a namespace
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secret-rotator
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: curl:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl && mkdir -p /logs"]
      containers:
      - name: rotator
        image: secret-rotator:latest
        env:
        - name: ROTATION_API
          value: https://rotation-api.local/rotate
        - name: API_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: rotation-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotence of a rotation? 
- What RBAC rules would you apply for the agent? 
- How would you handle API failures or partial rotations?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests end-to-end CKAD skills: per-namespace scoping, InitContainers, in-cluster secret handling, result storage via ConfigMap/Secret, and network policies. Encourages concrete YAML design rather than abstract concepts.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainers for tool setup
- In-namespace Secret/ConfigMap usage
- In-cluster traffic control with NetworkPolicy
- Sidecar for TLS cert rotation
- Post/aggregate results in-cluster

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton (Deployment, Secret, ConfigMap placeholders)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: registry-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  username: <base64>
  password: <base64>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: image-scan-config
data:
  registry: my-registry.io
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache trivy; mkdir -p /tools"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: images
          mountPath: /images
      containers:
      - name: scanner
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "while read img; do trivy image $img --format json >> /reports/scan.json; done < /images/list.txt"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: images
          mountPath: /images
      volumes:
      - name: images
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: images-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test this in a namespace with multiple image formats and large lists?
- What changes would you make to handle authentication failures and rate-limiting?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses the ability to design a namespace-scoped canary workflow using standard CKAD primitives: CronJob, ConfigMaps, and Deployment rolling updates. It also tests observability knowledge via PVC-backed logs, status tracking patterns, and security awareness through NetworkPolicy and InitContainer usage.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMaps**: canary-config holds dynamic parameters (targetImage, canaryPercent); canary-status records rollout history and last-promotion timestamps
- **CronJob**: Provides periodic reconciliation that checks configuration and triggers conditional updates
- **Deployment RollingUpdate**: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 ensures controlled, non-disruptive updates
- **Traffic Shifting**: Routes a configurable percentage of traffic to canary pods for gradual exposure
- **InitContainer**: Ensures jq availability for JSON parsing within the job
- **Probes**: Readiness gates ensure traffic only reaches healthy pods; liveness checks restart unhealthy instances
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricts namespace egress to approved registries only
- **PVC**: Persists job logs for debugging and audit trails

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Fully Kubernetes-native with no external dependencies; ConfigMap history provides auditability; automatic promotion reduces manual intervention
- **Cons**: Namespace-scoped only; NetworkPolicy requires CNI support; jq dependency increases image size; ConfigMaps lack built-in validation

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of namespace-scoped quotas and limits, basic RBAC implications, and how quotas affect scheduling.

## Key Concepts
- ResourceQuota
- LimitRange
- Namespace NetworkPolicy
- Scheduling under quotas

## Code Example
````yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    limits.cpu: '4'
    limits.memory: '8Gi'
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-limit
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: '500m'
      memory: '256Mi'
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: '100m'
      memory: '128Mi'
    max:
      cpu: '2'
      memory: '2Gi'
    min:
      cpu: '100m'
      memory: '128Mi'
    type: Container
---
# Deployment (tests quota)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:alpine
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: '250m'
            memory: '256Mi'
          limits:
            cpu: '500m'
            memory: '512Mi'
---
# NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-internal-egress
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
````

## Why This Is Asked

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal patch skeleton (conceptual)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: worker
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<computed-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: myorg/worker:latest
          securityContext:
            runAsUser: 1000
            runAsGroup: 1000
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          env: []
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health

            - name: data

            - name: config

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives and their impact on scheduling, pod density, and autoscaler behavior.

## Key Concepts
- **ResourceQuota** enforces hard caps on total namespace resource consumption (CPU, memory, pod count, etc.)
- **LimitRange** sets defaults and constraints for individual pod/container resource requests and limits
- Quota enforcement affects scheduler decisions, pod scheduling failures, and autoscaler calculations
- Use `kubectl describe resourcequota <name> --namespace=<ns>` and `kubectl top pod` to monitor usage

## Code Example

```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: quota-demo
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: ns-quota
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
    pods: "20"
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: ns-limits
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 250m
      memory: 256Mi
    max:
      cpu: "2"
      memory: "4Gi"
    min:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
---
# Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: quota-demo-app
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 128Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 512Mi
```

## Trade-offs
- **Flexibility vs. Control**: Quotas prevent resource hoarding but require developers to specify requests/limits, increasing YAML complexity
- **Utilization Risk**: Overly restrictive quotas lead to pod scheduling failures; overly generous quotas waste resources
- **Debugging Overhead**: Quota-induced failures (e.g., "pods quota exceeded") add a layer of complexity to troubleshooting
- **Autoscaler Interaction**: VPA/HPA behavior changes when quotas constrain available headroom

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of the sidecar pattern for config reloading without full pod restarts.

## Key Concepts
- Sidecar container pattern
- inotify for file system monitoring
- SIGHUP for process signal handling
- ConfigMap mounting and reload behavior
- Zero-downtime configuration updates

## Patch Example
```yaml
# payments/processor-deployment.yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: config-watcher
          image: busybox:stable
          command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              apk add --no-cache inotify-tools
              inotifywait -m -e modify -r /etc/processor |
              while read path event; do
                kill -HUP 1
              done
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 65534
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/processor
              readOnly: true
```

## Verification Under Load
1. Apply patch and verify pod rollout: `kubectl rollout status deployment/processor -n payments`
2. Simulate ConfigMap update: `kubectl create configmap processor-config --from-literal=data=updated --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`
3. Verify sidecar detects change: `kubectl logs processor-<pod> -c config-watcher -n payments`
4. Confirm main process reloads: check application logs for reload indicators
5. Load test with tools like `hey` or `wrk` to verify zero downtime during reload

## Rollback Procedure
1. `kubectl rollout undo deployment/processor -n payments`
2. Verify previous version: `kubectl rollout status deployment/processor -n payments`
3. Confirm stable state: `kubectl get pods -n payments -l app=processor`

## Why This Is Asked
This CKAD-level question tests comprehensive Kubernetes skills by requiring a complete ETL pipeline implementation with production-ready features including security, reliability, and observability.

## Key Concepts
- **CronJob Management**: Scheduling, concurrency control, and failure handling policies
- **Security Context**: Non-root execution and least privilege principles
- **Volume Management**: Secret, ConfigMap, and PVC mounting strategies
- **Health Monitoring**: Readiness and liveness probes for application reliability
- **Lifecycle Management**: PreStop hooks for graceful shutdown
- **High Availability**: PodDisruptionBudget for maintenance safety

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-processor
  namespace: etl
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  backoffLimit: 3
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
          serviceAccountName: etl-runner
          volumes:
          - name: db-creds
            secret:
              secretName: db-creds
          - name: etl-config
            configMap:
              name: etl-config
          - name: etl-output
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: etl-output
          containers:
          - name: processor
            image: your-processor-image:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: db-creds
              mountPath: /etc/creds
              readOnly: true
            - name: etl-config
              mountPath: /etc/etl/config
              readOnly: true
            - name: etl-output
              mountPath: /data
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /livez
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /readyz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: daily-processor-pdb
  namespace: etl
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: daily-processor

Use `kubectl rollout history` to track changes, `kubectl rollout undo` for immediate rollback, and maintain multiple deployment versions for staged rollouts. Test rollback procedures in non-production environments before production deployment.

          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache sqlite"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: db
              mountPath: /data
          containers:
          - name: pruner
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh", "-c", "sqlite3 /data/logs.db 'DELETE FROM logs WHERE created_at < date(\"now\", \"-30 days\"); VACUUM;'; curl -X POST -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" -d '{\"deleted\":\"$(date)\"}' http://ops-portal:8080/api/v1/prune-summary"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: db
              mountPath: /data
            resources:
              requests:
                memory: "64Mi"
                cpu: "100m"
              limits:
                memory: "128Mi"
                cpu: "500m"
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]
          volumes:
          - name: db
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: log-pruner-pdb
  namespace: ckad-practices
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-pruner
```

## Rollback Strategy
Maintain version-controlled YAML manifests in a Git repository. On failure, execute:
```bash
kubectl apply -f log-pruner.yaml --record
kubectl rollout undo cronjob/log-pruner
```
Alternatively, use a GitOps tool like ArgoCD or Flux for automated rollbacks.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question validates understanding of CronJob mechanics, ConfigMap/Secret consumption, storage semantics, NetworkPolicy egress rules, and health probe configuration—core CKAD competencies.

## Key Design Decisions

### 1. CronJob Configuration
- **schedule**: `*/5 * * * *` runs every 5 minutes
- **concurrencyPolicy: Forbid** prevents overlapping job executions
- **backoffLimit: 2** limits retry attempts on failure

### 2. initContainer Pattern
The initContainer installs Python dependencies (`kubernetes`, `requests`) into an `emptyDir` volume before the main container starts. This ensures:
- Dependencies available at runtime
- Shared volume (`/tools`) accessible to both containers

### 3. Secret Mounting
Secrets are mounted as read-only volumes (`/secrets/api-token`), not just environment variables. This:
- Prevents accidental exposure in `kubectl describe pod`
- Allows file-based access in Python script
- Follows security best practices

### 4. NetworkPolicy Egress
```yaml
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector: {}  # All namespaces
  ports:
  - port: 443              # Webhook endpoint
- to:
  - namespaceSelector: {}
  ports:
  - port: 53               # DNS (required for name resolution)
```

### 5. Health Probes
- **readinessProbe**: Checks if container can serve traffic (HTTP GET on `/healthz`)
- **livenessProbe**: Checks if container needs restart (HTTP GET on `/healthz`)
- Proper `initialDelaySeconds` prevents premature failures during startup

### 6. Security Contexts
- `runAsNonRoot: true` with `runAsUser: 1000`
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` prevents container from writing to filesystem
- Resource limits prevent resource exhaustion

### 7. Python Script Logic
- Loads in-cluster config for Kubernetes API access
- Reads `LABEL_SELECTOR` from ConfigMap volume
- Fetches Warning events using field and label selectors
- Logs structured JSON to PVC-mounted `/logs`
- Posts summary to webhook with Bearer token authentication

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical security hardening and disruption management capabilities for CKAD-level Kubernetes deployments.

## Key Concepts
- Container SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem for container isolation
- PodSecurityContext: fsGroup for proper file permissions on PVC-mounted volumes
- Kernel capabilities: drop ALL to minimize attack surface
- PodDisruptionBudget: maintain minimum healthy pods during maintenance
- Rollout and rollback procedures for safe deployments

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  labels:
    app: api-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-gateway
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 1001
      containers:
      - name: api-gateway
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - "ALL"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /srv
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/app
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: api-gateway-pvc
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: api-gateway-config
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api-gateway-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-gateway
```

## Verification & Rollback
```bash
# Verify under load
kubectl exec deployment/api-gateway -- curl http://localhost:8080/health
kubectl top pods -l app=api-gateway
kubectl get pods -l app=api-gateway --watch

# Rollback if needed
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-gateway
kubectl rollout status deployment/api-gateway
```
